concepts.description: Keeping trees shallow by hanging the smaller tree under the larger.

concepts.name: Offline vs online
concepts.description: DSU handles edges as they arrive, without needing the full graph upfront.

patterns.name: Iterative DSU find
patterns.description: Path-halving version of find that avoids recursion limits.

patterns.name: Class-based DSU with component size
patterns.description: Object-oriented wrapper that also exposes set sizes.

examples.title: Friends groups
examples.problem: There are 4 people; friendships (0,1) and (1,2). How many friend groups?
examples.explanation: People 0,1,2 form one group; person 3 is alone.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to compress paths, causing find to degrade to O(N).
mistakes.fix: Apply path compression inside find on every call.

mistakes.mistake: Unioning when the elements already share a root, needlessly corrupting rank data.
mistakes.fix: Short-circuit union when find(a) == find(b).

mistakes.mistake: Using 1-indexed input with a 0-indexed parent array.
mistakes.fix: Size the arrays to n + 1 or normalize indices to 0.

problems.name: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
problems.description: Count the connected components of an undirected graph.
hints: Union every edge.
Count distinct roots at the end.
problems.approach: DSU over all nodes, then count unique roots.
problems.solution: Create a DSU with n nodes and union the endpoints of every edge. After all unions, the number of components equals the number of distinct root values among the n nodes.

problems.name: Redundant Connection II
problems.description: Given a directed graph that is a tree plus one extra edge, return the edge that, when removed, makes it a valid rooted tree.
hints: Two failure modes: a node with two parents, or a cycle.
Check both conditions with DSU.
problems.approach: Detect the conflicting edge with two parents; otherwise find the edge that closes a cycle using DSU.
problems.solution: Scan edges tracking parent counts. If a node has two parents, keep both candidate edges. Otherwise, run DSU over the edges: the first edge whose endpoints already share a root is the cycle edge. If both a two-parent conflict and a cycle exist, remove the two-parent candidate inside the cycle; otherwise remove the appropriate candidate.

problems.name: Number of Operations to Make Network Connected
problems.description: Given n computers and cable connections, return the minimum number of cables to move to connect all computers, or -1 if impossible.
hints: Connecting c components needs c - 1 extra cables.
Count components with DSU.
problems.approach: DSU to count components and extra edges; answer is components - 1 if enough spare cables exist.
problems.solution: Union every connection; count redundant edges (those whose endpoints are already connected) and the number of components. If redundant edges are fewer than components - 1, return -1. Otherwise return components - 1, which is exactly the number of cables that must be moved.

name: Advanced graph algorithms
overview: Advanced graph algorithms extend the basics with specialized machinery: strongly connected components, bridges and articulation points, Eulerian paths, maximum flow, and graph coloring.
why: These algorithms unlock hard and premium interview problems and demonstrate mastery of graph theory when a plain traversal is not enough.
when: Use them for structural decompositions (SCC, bridges), path existence constraints (Eulerian), resource allocation (flow, matching), and constraint satisfaction (coloring).

complexity.time: Varies: O(V + E) for Tarjan, O(V * E^2) for Dinic flow

concepts.name: Eulerian path
concepts.description: A path that uses every edge exactly once; exists based on vertex degree parity.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian path
concepts.description: A path that visits every vertex exactly once; NP-hard in general.

concepts.name: Maximum flow
concepts.description: The largest amount of flow that can be sent from source to sink in a capacitated network.

concepts.name: Graph coloring
concepts.description: Assigning colors to vertices so adjacent vertices differ; bipartiteness is 2-coloring.

concepts.name: Dinic's algorithm
concepts.description: Blocking-flow algorithm computing max flow in O(V^2 * E) or better with unit capacities.

concepts.name: Low-link decomposition
concepts.description: Discovering bridges, articulation points, and SCCs via discovery/low-link times.

patterns.name: Dinic max flow
patterns.description: BFS for level graph plus DFS blocking flows, repeated until no augmenting path.

patterns.name: Hierholzer Eulerian path
patterns.description: Follow unused edges and splice cycles to build an Eulerian trail.

examples.title: Eulerian path in a graph
examples.problem: Does the graph with edges (0,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,3) have an Eulerian path?
examples.explanation: Degrees are 0:2, 1:2, 2:3, 3:1. An Eulerian path needs zero or exactly two odd-degree vertices, but this graph has two odd vertices, so a path exists. (A trail using all edges exists with endpoints 3 and 2.)
steps: Count odd-degree vertices: vertices 2 and 3 (two of them).
Two odd vertices means an Eulerian trail exists.
Start at one odd vertex and trace edges until all are used.
A closed Eulerian circuit requires all even degrees.

mistakes.mistake: Attempting Hamiltonian path search on large graphs and hitting exponential blowups.
mistakes.fix: Recognize Hamiltonian problems as NP-hard and use heuristics or small-n DP (Held-Karp).

mistakes.mistake: Using BFS/DFS where a max-flow reduction is required.
mistakes.fix: Model resource allocation and cut problems as flow networks and run Dinic or Edmonds-Karp.

mistakes.mistake: Treating every directed graph cycle problem as an SCC problem and vice versa.
mistakes.fix: Use cycle detection for yes/no cycle queries and SCC for decomposing the graph.

problems.name: Course Schedule with Multiple Requirements
problems.description: Given courses with capacity and student preferences, determine if every student can be assigned while respecting course limits.
problems.constraints: Moderate sizes; represents a bipartite matching with capacities.
hints: Model as a flow network: source to students, students to courses, courses to sink.
Max flow equals number of students iff assignment is possible.
problems.approach: Reduce to maximum flow and check whether the flow saturates all students.
problems.solution: Build a flow network: connect a source to every student with capacity 1, each student to their preferred courses with capacity 1, and each course to the sink with its capacity. Run max flow. If the total flow equals the number of students, every student is assigned; otherwise the assignment is impossible.

problems.name: Reconstruct Itinerary
problems.description: Given a list of airline tickets, find the itinerary that uses every ticket exactly once starting from JFK, with the smallest lexical order.
hints: This is an Eulerian path problem.
Use Hierholzer's algorithm with a heap to keep order.
problems.approach: Hierholzer's algorithm: DFS over edges, appending nodes on backtrack, then reverse.
problems.solution: Build an adjacency list where each airport's destinations are kept in a min-heap for lexical order. Run Hierholzer: from JFK, repeatedly take the smallest unused edge. When a node has no edges left, append it to the result; after the DFS, reverse the result to get the itinerary that uses every ticket exactly once.

problems.name: Minimum Number of Colors for a Graph
problems.description: Color the vertices of a graph so no two adjacent vertices share a color, using as few colors as possible.
problems.constraints: Small graphs; general coloring is NP-hard.
hints: If the graph is bipartite, 2 colors suffice.
Otherwise greedy coloring gives an upper bound; try to minimize.
problems.approach: Try 2 colors first via bipartite check, then greedy coloring for more colors.
problems.time: O(V + E) for bipartite, greedy O(V^2) worst case
problems.solution: First test bipartiteness with BFS/DFS; if two colors work, return 2. Otherwise apply a greedy algorithm: order vertices, assign each the smallest color not used by its colored neighbors. While greedy may not be optimal in general, for small structured inputs it often matches the chromatic number.

name: Advanced graph theory
overview: Advanced graph theory covers the deeper structural ideas that power hard problems: graph cuts, connectivity metrics, planar and tree properties, and how reductions transform problems into known graph tasks.
why: Recognizing these underlying structures lets you solve problems that look unrelated, and interviewers value the insight that 'this is a graph problem'.
when: Use graph-theoretic reasoning when a problem involves network robustness, minimum cuts, hierarchical grouping, or constraint modeling that is not a plain traversal.

complexity.time: Varies by problem; reductions often change the complexity class

concepts.name: Graph cut
concepts.description: A partition of vertices into two sets; the cut edges cross the boundary.

concepts.name: Min-cut / max-flow duality
concepts.description: The minimum cut capacity equals the maximum flow by the max-flow min-cut theorem.

concepts.name: k-connected graph
concepts.description: A graph that stays connected after removing any k-1 vertices.

concepts.name: Graph coloring bounds
concepts.description: Every planar graph is 4-colorable; chromatic number links to clique size.

concepts.name: Treewidth
concepts.description: A measure of how tree-like a graph is; low treewidth enables efficient DP.

concepts.name: Problem reduction
concepts.description: Translating a novel problem into a known graph problem like matching or flow.

patterns.name: Reachability via BFS as a yes/no model
patterns.description: Many problems reduce to checking reachability on a transformed state graph.

patterns.name: Vertex splitting for node capacities
patterns.description: Convert node capacities into edge capacities for flow problems.

examples.title: Min-cut in a small network
examples.problem: Network with source 0, sink 3, and edges 0->1(3), 0->2(2), 1->3(2), 2->3(3), 1->2(1). What is the min cut?
examples.explanation: The max flow equals the min cut. Sending 2 via 0->2->3 and 2 via 0->1->3 plus 1 via 0->1->2->3 gives a total flow of 5; the cut ({0}, {1,2,3}) has capacity 3 + 2 = 5.
steps: The flow saturates the edges leaving the source side.
The saturated cut {0} vs the rest has capacity 5.
By the max-flow min-cut theorem this equals the min cut.
No smaller cut exists, so the answer is 5.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming min cut requires enumerating all 2^V partitions.
mistakes.fix: Use max-flow algorithms to find the min cut in polynomial time.

mistakes.mistake: Believing every graph problem maps to a simple known algorithm.
mistakes.fix: Learn when reductions apply and when problems are NP-hard.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring edge cases like empty graphs, single vertices, and disconnected inputs in theory-based problems.
mistakes.fix: Check connectivity and small inputs before reasoning about global structure.

problems.name: Maximum Network Reliability
problems.description: Given a network and a target pair of servers, find the minimum number of connections whose removal would disconnect them.
problems.constraints: Moderate sized networks; edges have unit capacity.
hints: The answer is the size of the minimum cut.
Unit-capacity min cut equals max flow with unit edges.
problems.approach: Model connections as unit-capacity edges and compute max flow between the pair.
problems.solution: Build a flow network where every connection is an undirected edge with capacity 1. Compute max flow between the two servers. By the max-flow min-cut theorem, the value equals the minimum number of edges that must be removed to disconnect them.

problems.name: City Planning Connectivity
problems.description: Given a grid of blocks, determine whether two blocks are connected through a walk that uses at most k turns.
problems.constraints: Grid up to a few hundred cells.
hints: Expand each cell into states by direction and turn count.
Run BFS on the expanded state graph.
problems.approach: Build a state graph (cell, direction, turns) and BFS to the target state within the turn budget.
problems.solution: Create a node for each (cell, direction, turnsUsed) combination. Moving straight keeps the direction and turns; turning increments the turn count. BFS from the start cell in all four directions, tracking the minimal turns to each state. If the target cell is reached with at most k turns, return true; otherwise false.

problems.name: Minimum Cut to Isolate a Region
problems.description: Given a grid of weighted cells, find the minimum total weight of cells to remove so the region is separated into two parts.
problems.constraints: Small grids with weights on cells.
hints: Split each cell into in/out nodes with its weight as the edge.
Run min-cut with the split nodes.
problems.approach: Vertex-splitting transformation plus max-flow to find the minimum weighted vertex cut.
problems.solution: Replace each cell with two nodes (in, out) joined by an edge of capacity equal to the cell's weight; connect adjacent cells by infinite-capacity edges from out to in. Add a super source and sink connected to the boundary cells. The max flow equals the minimum weight of cells that must be removed to disconnect the region.
